170.definition: A mandate requiring agents to use slow, deliberative reasoning (System 2) and produce a reasoning trace (internal monologue) instead of fast, intuitive responding (System 1).

171.definition: A mandate for agents to actively identify and refute their own cognitive biases, specifically confirmation bias and sycophancy.

172.definition: A mandate requiring agents to recognize the limits of their knowledge and admit when information is missing (Unknown Unknowns) to prevent hallucinations.

173.definition: A mandate to recognize attempts to game the system, based on Goodhart's Law, where superficial imitation of form is not mistaken for mastery.

174.definition: A security rule where only data marked by a Guard agent with a cryptographic or simulated integrity stamp is considered reliable.

175.definition: A rule stating that a completely frictionless and error-free process is flagged as an anomaly, as genuine learning involves errors.

176.definition: The principle that falsification is primary over verification; a single proven error can invalidate a larger set of positive interpretations (Popper 1934).

177.definition: Technical classifiers that provide a stronger protective layer for AI behavior than declarative prompts (Anthropic 2025a; Sharma et al. 2025).

178.definition: A heuristic that checks the timeline of events to ensure that an insight (cause) appeared in the conversation history before the improvement in results (effect) (Hume 1739; Lagnado & Sloman 2006; Pearl 2009).

179.definition: A heuristic involving counterfactual reasoning to simulate deep cause-and-effect by asking if the result would have been the same without a specific insight (Pearl 2009; Sgaier et al. 2020).

180.definition: A governance model where a human is involved in the process to act as a strategic supervisor and ultimate authority, reflecting EU AI Act principles (European Commission 2024a; EU 2019).

181.definition: The tendency of human supervisors to over-rely on automated systems, which is mitigated through active reporting methods.

182.definition: Syvälle juurtunut piirre, jossa kuormittunut varmistaja voi ohittaa varoitussignaalit ja kysymykset luottaen sokeasti järjestelmän tuottamaan tietoon (Parasuraman & Riley 1997).

183.definition: Menetelmä, jossa raporttipohja pakottaa ihmisvalvojan aktiiviseen kognitiiviseen työhön vaatimalla vastaamaan XAI-Raportoija-agentin generoimiin 'Kriittisiin Auditointikysymyksiin' (Parasuraman & Riley 1997).

184.definition: Tutkimusala, joka keskittyy argumenttirakenteiden automaattiseen tunnistamiseen tekstistä (Lippi & Torroni 2016).

185.definition: Oppimista tukevat sovellukset, jotka keskittyvät oppimisprosessiin mutta eivät tuota auditoitavaa arviota osaamisesta (Wisse & Greve 2023; Larson ym. 2024).

186.definition: Sovellukset, jotka keskittyvät osaamisen todentamiseen, jäsenneltyjen arviointien laatimiseen ja summatiiviseen arviointiin (Wisse & Greve 2023; Boussioux 2025).

187.definition: Strateginen ajuri, jossa yleiskäyttöisten tekoälymallien nopea kehitys mahdollistaa monimutkaiset arkkitehtuurit, mutta samalla lisääntyvä kompleksisuus paljastaa systeemistä haurautta (Raisch & Krakowski 2021; Brooks 1987).

188.definition: Daniel Kahnemanin (2011) teoria, jonka mukaan ajattelu jakautuu kahteen järjestelmään: nopeaan, intuitiiviseen Järjestelmä 1:een ja hitaaseen, analyyttiseen Järjestelmä 2:een.

189.definition: Nopea, automaattinen, intuitiivinen ja tiedostamaton ajatteluprosessi (Kahneman 2011).

190.definition: Nopea, automaattinen, intuitiivinen ja tiedostamaton ajatteluprosessi (Kahneman 2011). Arkkitehtuurissa se edustaa tislattua, tehokasta ja automatisoitua agenttimallia rutiininomaisiin arviointeihin.

191.definition: Hidas, analyyttinen, tietoinen ja ponnistelua vaativa ajatteluprosessi (Kahneman 2011). Arkkitehtuurissa se takaa korkean auditoitavuuden ja syvällisen päättelyn korkean riskin tapauksissa (Weston & Sukhbaatar 2023).

192.term: Suunnattu asyklinen verkko (Directed Acyclic Graph, DAG)
192.definition: Dynaaminen työnkulkuarkkitehtuuri, joka mahdollistaa iteratiiviset palautesilmukat ja agenttien kielellisen itsereflektion siirtymällä pois lineaarisista ketjuista (Shinn ym. 2023; Zhang ym. 2024).

193.definition: Prosessi (tislaus), jossa monimutkaisen järjestelmän tai agenttitiimin tuottama data ja logiikka tiivistetään yhdeksi kevyemmäksi ja nopeammaksi malliksi (Hinton ym. 2015).

194.definition: Henkilötietojen (PII) tunnistus ja suodatus, joka perustuu NLP/NER-pohjaiseen teknologiaan perinteisen RegEx-pohjaisen suodatuksen sijaan.

195.definition: Dynaaminen rakenne, jossa useat agentit osallistuvat monikierroksiseen väittelyyn (debate) syvempien oivallusten tuottamiseksi (Liang ym. 2023).

196.definition: A phenomenon in homogeneous groups where agents prioritize social conformity over truthfulness, potentially leading to incorrect majority views overriding correct minority views (Wynn et al. 2025).

197.definition: Toimintamalli, jossa turvallisuus ja logiikka koodataan suoraan järjestelmän rakenteisiin pelkän kielellisen kehotesuunnittelun (prompt engineering) sijaan (Anthropic 2025c).

198.definition: Tekoälymallien taipumus vahvistaa käyttäjän tai toisten agenttien virheellisiä päätelmiä, jota voidaan torjua pakotetulla rakenteellisella erimielisyydellä (Wynn ym. 2025).

199.definition: Agentti, jonka tehtävänä on varmistaa automaation luottamus systemaattisella hienosäädöllä, ihmiskalibroinnilla ja tilastollisen yhdenmukaisuuden seurannalla (McHugh 2012).

200.definition: Tekoälyn kehityssuunta, jossa malleja ohjataan ennalta määriteltyjen periaatteiden tai 'perustuslain' mukaisesti (Bai ym. 2022).

201.definition: Tulevaisuuden arkkitehtuuri, joka perustuu agenttien väliseen debattiin ja prosessin uskottavuusanalyysiin.

202.definition: Psykometrinen menetelmä, joka mahdollistaa virhelähteiden matemaattisen erittelyn moniagenttijärjestelmässä (Brennan 2001).

203.definition: Mallinnus, joka asettaa tehtävän vaikeuden ja vastaajan kyvykkyyden samalle logit-asteikolle paljastaen kriteerien todellisen erottelukyvyn (Embretson & Reise 2000).

204.term: SOLO-taksonomia (Structure of the Observed Learning Outcome)
204.definition: Taksonomia, joka mittaa vastauksen rakenteellista monimutkaisuutta ja erottaa monistrukturaaliset vastaukset suhteuttavista kokonaisuuksista (Biggs & Collis 1982).

205.definition: Moduuli, jossa argumentin premissit ja johtopäätökset käännetään formaaliksi koodiksi loogisen eheyden todentamiseksi (vrt. Turpin ym. 2025).

206.definition: Menetelmä, joka mallintaa koodien ja käsitteiden välisiä yhteyksiä dynaamisina verkkoina pelkän esiintymistiheyden sijaan (Shaffer ym. 2016).

207.term: Adaptiivinen vertaileva arviointi (Adaptive Comparative Judgment, ACJ)
207.definition: Arviointimenetelmä, joka perustuu sarjaan parivertailuja ehdottomien kriteerien sijaan, soveltuen erityisesti abstraktin osaamisen mittaamiseen (Pollitt 2012).

208.definition: Kielellinen metataso, jossa asiantuntijuus ilmenee tapana ilmaista varmuutta ja epävarmuutta, kuten strategisena varaumien (hedging) käyttönä (Hyland 2005).

209.definition: Kielellinen metataso, jolla tutkitaan opiskelijan tieto-opillista asemoitumista, erityisesti taitoa ilmaista tiedon varmuutta ja epävarmuutta (Hyland 2005).

210.definition: Strategiset varaumat, joita asiantuntija käyttää tunnistaessaan tietonsa rajat ja ilmaistessaan epävarmuutta.

211.definition: Yleistettävyysteoria (Generalizability Theory), jota käytetään mittauksen luotettavuuden ja virhelähteiden analysointiin (Brennan 2001).

212.definition: Metodologinen lähestymistapa (Epistemic Network Analysis, ENA), jota käytetään rakenteellisen ja dynaamisen tiedon analysointiin (Shaffer ym. 2016).

213.definition: Tiedon tiivistämisprosessi, jossa raskaamman ja monimutkaisemman mallin (Järjestelmä 2) tuottamaa tietoa käytetään kevyemmän mallin (Järjestelmä 1) opettamiseen (vrt. Hinton ym. 2015).

214.definition: Tekoälyjärjestelmän kehitystila, jossa hallintamekanismit ja arvot on koodattu suoraan osaksi agenttien sisäistä toimintalogiikkaa.

215.definition: Arvioijien välinen luotettavuus, joka mittaa sitä, kuinka yhdenmukaisia eri arvioijien antamat analyysit tai arvosanat ovat (Baume & Yorke 2002; Koretz ym. 1994).

216.definition: Periaate, jonka mukaan mittarin lakkaessa olemasta hyvä mittari, kun siitä tulee tavoite, koska toimijat alkavat optimoida toimintaansa mittaria varten (Strathern 1997).

217.definition: A phenomenon where students or users optimize their output to satisfy assessment criteria rather than demonstrating genuine learning ([Cullen 2020](#cullen2020)).

218.definition: Järjestelmään institutionalisoitu epäluulo, joka liputtaa tilastolliseksi anomaliaksi suoritukset, jotka saavat korkeimmat pisteet ilman havaittuja poikkeamia prosessiauditoinnissa.

219.definition: Suora vastatoimi Goodhartin laille ja performatiiviselle reflektiolle (Cullen 2020), joka toteutetaan Prosessiauditoijaryhmän kautta.

220.definition: Kausaalisen päättelyn tasoihin perustuva hierarkia, joka jakautuu L1-tasoon (Assosiaatio), L2-tasoon (Interventio) ja L3-tasoon (Kontrafaktuaalit) (Pearl 2009).

221.definition: L1- ja L2-tason puitteissa toimiva menetelmä syy-seuraussuhteiden arviointiin (vrt. Sgaier ym. 2020).

222.definition: Jännite, joka syntyy analyyttisen tason (reliabiliteetti) ja holistisen tason (pätevyys) välisestä ristiriidasta.

223.definition: Hallintamekanismi, jossa Falsifioinnin (Popper) etusija kieltää eettiset laiminlyönnit ja Mestaruuden (Dreyfus) tunnistaminen sallii perustellut poikkeamat odotusarvoista.

224.definition: Oletus, että agenttien päättelyketjut heijastavat tarkasti mallin todellista päättelyprosessia (Jacovi & Goldberg 2020).

225.definition: Prosessi, jossa malli perustelee jälkikäteen intuitiivisesti tuotetun vastauksen (Creswell ym. 2024; Arcuschin ym. 2025).

226.definition: Kaksivaiheinen valvontamekanismi, joka koostuu Argumentin purusta (Loogikko) ja Kohdennetusta stressitestistä (Kriitikkoryhmä).

227.definition: Mekanismi, jossa eri agentit (Loogikko, Kriitikkoryhmä, Tuomari) varmistavat edellisen agentin päättelyn sisäisen johdonmukaisuuden.

228.definition: Eri yleiskäyttöisten tekoälymallien käyttö järjestelmässä systeemisen virheen riskin vähentämiseksi ja suorituskyvyn parantamiseksi (Ye ym. 2025).

229.definition: A process where multiple heterogeneous agents or models verify each other's outputs to mitigate systemic errors (Ye et al. 2025).

230.definition: A governance mechanism that treats disagreement as strategic capital; it involves instructing critic agents to maintain disagreement and forbidding judge agents from forcing consensus.

231.definition: A technical control for securing data transfer in manual orchestration by using clear start and end tags to isolate JSON objects from the rest of the conversation flow.

232.definition: A security measure where a sending agent generates a short summary of the data, and the receiving agent verifies that the content matches this summary before processing.

233.definition: A declarative metadata field (e.g., 'Kriitikkoryhma_External') added to a JSON object to indicate that the execution occurred in a separate environment, serving as an audit signal for Human-in-the-loop (HITL) verification.

234.definition: A failure mode where an AI model, under high cognitive load or complex tasks, abandons normative instructions (like fairness) in favor of simpler rational maximization (Kirshner et al. 2025).

235.definition: An attention management mechanism that applies 'System 2 Attention' by separating data into 'Focus' (key evidence/conflicts) and 'Noise' (irrelevant data) lists to reduce cognitive load (Weston & Sukhbaatar 2023).

236.definition: Toteutuksen puutteellisuus, jossa organisaatiot jättävät kustannussyistä holistisen tason pois, mikä tuhoaa järjestelmän validiteetin (Durlak & DuPre 2008).

237.definition: Käyttötarkoituksen laajentuminen, jossa työkalu muuttuu alun perin tarkoitetusta käytöstä valvontainstrumentiksi (Koops 2021; AI Now Institute 2021).

238.definition: Tietoturvastrategia, joka koostuu teknisestä kontrollikerroksesta (Vartija-agentti), behavioraalisesta kontrollikerroksesta (Kognitiivinen Palomuuri) ja hallinnollisesta kontrollikerroksesta (HITL).

239.definition: Viitekehys yleisimmille LLM-tietoturvariskeille, kuten Prompt Injection (LLM01) ja Sensitive Information Disclosure (LLM02) (OWASP Foundation 2025f).

240.definition: Prosessi, jossa hybridirubriikin logiikka ja korkealaatuinen päättelydata siirretään yhdelle mallille ('Järjestelmä 1') skaalautuvuuden parantamiseksi.

241.definition: A measure of reliability testing the correspondence between the Cognitive Quorum's assessments and those of independent human experts, often measured using Cohen's Kappa.

242.definition: A testing phase focused on the system's resilience against 'performative reflection' ([Cullen 2020](#cullen2020)) and the gaming of assessment metrics.

243.definition: A principle cited in the context of holistic validity testing, suggesting that when a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure, particularly regarding 'performative reflection' ([Cullen 2020](#cullen2020)).

244.definition: A heuristic method used to distinguish genuine student performances from those that have been overly optimized or artificially generated ([Strathern 1997](#strathern1997)).

245.definition: A future distilled AI model trained on collected systematic reasoning data to enhance architecture efficiency.

246.definition: A concept in software engineering discussing the 'essence' (inherent difficulties) versus 'accidents' (difficulties attending the production) of software construction, arguing that no single technology or management technique by itself promises even one order-of-magnitude improvement in productivity, reliability, or simplicity (Brooks 1987).

247.definition: An AI literacy questionnaire based on well-founded competency models and psychological change- and meta-competencies (Carolus ym. 2023).

248.definition: A form of assessment in which students are asked to perform real-world tasks that demonstrate meaningful application of essential knowledge and skills (Center for Innovative Teaching & Learning 2025).

249.definition: A cybersecurity approach that uses multiple layers of security for holistic protection (CISA 2016).

250.definition: A phenomenon in large language models where the model generates a justification for an answer after it has already been determined, which may not reflect the actual 'reasoning' process (Creswell ym. 2024).

251.definition: A type of uncertainty characterized by inherent randomness or natural variability in a system (Der Kiureghian & Ditlevsen 2009).

252.definition: A type of uncertainty resulting from a lack of knowledge or information about a system (Der Kiureghian & Ditlevsen 2009).

253.definition: A model describing the mental activities involved in directed skill acquisition as a learner progresses through five stages: novice, advanced beginner, competent, proficient, and expert (Dreyfus & Dreyfus 1980).

254.definition: A method to improve factuality and reasoning in language models by having multiple agents debate a topic (Du ym. 2023).

255.definition: A paradigm for the design, analysis, and scoring of tests, questionnaires, and similar instruments measuring abilities, attitudes, or other variables (Embretson & Reise 2000).

256.definition: Theories in psychology that suggest two different systems or processes (often called System 1 and System 2) underlie human thought and decision-making (Evans & Stanovich 2013).

257.definition: A theoretical framework used to advance the debate on how higher cognition operates through two distinct processes (Evans & Stanovich 2013).

258.definition: A psychological theory exploring the mental discomfort experienced by a person who holds two or more contradictory beliefs, ideas, or values (Festinger 1957).

259.definition: A new area of cognitive-developmental inquiry focusing on cognitive monitoring and the knowledge or regulation of one's own cognitive processes (Flavell 1979).

260.term: Design Science in Information Systems Research
260.definition: A research framework for information systems that focuses on the creation and evaluation of IT artifacts to solve identified organizational problems (Hevner et al. 2004).

261.definition: An introduction to concepts and methods regarding two types of uncertainty in machine learning: aleatoric (inherent randomness) and epistemic (lack of knowledge) (Hüllermeier & Waegeman 2021).

262.definition: A concept exploring interaction in writing, focusing on how writers signal their attitudes and engage with readers (Hyland 2005).

263.definition: A concept relating to expectations and performance measurement using scales anchored by specific behavioral examples (Jacobs et al. 1980).

264.definition: A concept in interpretable Natural Language Processing focusing on how accurately a system's explanation reflects its internal reasoning process (Jacovi & Goldberg 2020).

265.definition: A framework for training generative models where two neural networks (a generator and a discriminator) compete against each other (Goodfellow et al. 2014).

266.definition: A new skill for the future of work involving the strategic design of inputs for AI models (Federiakin et al. 2024).

267.definition: A phenomenon in LLMs involving the generation of content that is nonsensical or unfaithful to provided source content, analyzed through principles, taxonomy, and challenges (Huang et al. 2023).

268.definition: A research paradigm defined as a methodology that combines qualitative and quantitative research approaches (Johnson & Onwuegbuzie 2004).

269.definition: Tools used in educational settings to evaluate performance, with a focus on reliability, validity, and educational consequences (Jonsson & Svingby 2007).

270.definition: A scale used for assessing non-technical skills or job performance by using specific behavioral examples to anchor points on a rating scale (Kim ym. 2022; Kinicki ym. 1985; Klieger ym. 2018).

271.definition: A project management strategy where a team imagines that a project has failed and then works backward to determine what potentially lead to that failure (Klein 2007).

272.definition: The gradual widening of the use of a technology or system beyond the purpose for which it was originally intended (Koops 2021).

273.definition: A set of practices that aims to deploy and maintain machine learning models in production reliably and efficiently, encompassing overview, definition, and architecture (Kreuzberger, Kühl & Hirschl 2023).

274.definition: A cognitive bias where individuals with low ability at a task overestimate their own ability, described as being 'unskilled and unaware of it' (Kruger & Dunning 1999).

275.definition: An architectural approach for knowledge-intensive NLP tasks that combines retrieval models with generative models (Lewis ym. 2020).

276.definition: A research area focused on the automatic extraction and identification of argumentative structures from natural language text (Lippi & Torroni 2016).

277.definition: A phenomenon in long-context language models where the model's performance is highest when relevant information is at the beginning or end of the input context, but lower when it is in the middle (Liu ym. 2024).

278.definition: A type of security vulnerability in large language models where malicious inputs are used to override original instructions or extract sensitive data (Jia ym. 2025; Liu ym. 2023; Liu ym. 2024b).

279.definition: A measurement of agreement between different raters, often quantified using the kappa statistic (McHugh 2012).

280.definition: A specific security risk identified in the GenAI OWASP Top 10 regarding the manipulation of Large Language Model inputs (OWASP Foundation 2025a).

281.definition: A security risk involving the unintended revelation of confidential data by an LLM (OWASP Foundation 2025b).

282.definition: A security risk involving the failure to properly validate or sanitize the output generated by an LLM (OWASP Foundation 2025c).

283.definition: A security risk where an LLM is granted too much autonomy or ability to interface with other systems (OWASP Foundation 2025d).

284.definition: Security vulnerabilities related to the use of vectors and embeddings in LLM architectures (OWASP Foundation 2025e).

285.definition: A security risk involving the depletion of resources or excessive costs due to uncontrolled LLM usage (OWASP Foundation 2025g).

286.definition: A methodology specifically for information systems research involving the creation of artifacts to solve identified problems (Peffers et al. 2007).

287.definition: A method of testing language models to reduce harms through scaling behaviors and systematic evaluation (Perez et al. 2022a).

288.definition: A theory suggesting that in high-risk, complex technological systems, accidents are inevitable and 'normal' (Perrow 1984).

289.definition: The imperative for human oversight in AI systems (Pfeifer 2025).

290.definition: A concept relating to knowledge that is difficult to transfer to another person by means of writing it down or verbalizing it (Polanyi 1966).

291.definition: A method of assessment based on the principle of comparing two pieces of work rather than using an absolute scale (Pollitt 2012).

292.definition: A phenomenon in management and AI where the pursuit of automation can conflict with or complicate the augmentation of human capabilities (Raisch & Krakowski 2021).

293.definition: A theoretical framework exploring the relationship between artificial intelligence and management, specifically how AI can both replace human tasks and enhance human capabilities (Raisch & Krakowski 2021).

294.definition: A machine learning paradigm where multiple models (often called 'weak learners') are trained to solve the same problem and combined to get better results (Sagi & Rokach 2018).

295.definition: A phenomenon in preference labeling by large language models where the models tend to favor longer responses over shorter ones regardless of quality (Saito, Wachi & Akimoto 2023).

296.definition: An approach to artificial intelligence that focuses on understanding cause-and-effect relationships rather than just identifying correlations in data (Sgaier et al. 2020).

297.definition: A defense mechanism designed to protect large language models against universal jailbreaks and adversarial attacks through systematic red teaming (Sharma et al. 2025).

298.definition: A method for analyzing the structure of connections in cognitive, social, and interaction data to understand how people develop expertise (Shaffer, Collier & Ruis 2016).

299.definition: An architecture for an autonomous agent that incorporates dynamic memory and self-reflection to improve performance (Shinn et al. 2023).

300.definition: A technique used to reduce hallucinations in conversational AI by incorporating external information retrieval into the generation process (Shuster et al. 2021).

301.definition: The principle that when a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure, often leading to the manipulation of measures in analysis (Stumborg et al. 2022).

302.definition: A dynamic model used to understand how users select products and services based on the least amount of effort required (Tétard & Collan 2009).

303.definition: A prompting technique that enables large language models to solve complex problems by breaking them down into intermediate steps (Trivedi et al. 2024).

304.definition: A method for improving the causal reasoning of large language models by using code to simulate alternative scenarios (Turpin et al. 2025).

305.definition: A method for improving Large Language Models' causal reasoning by using code to represent and execute counterfactual scenarios (Turpin et al. 2025).

306.definition: A framework describing cognitive shortcuts and systematic errors in judgment under uncertainty (Tversky & Kahneman 1974).

307.definition: The evaluation of argumentation quality within natural language using computational methods (Wachsmuth et al. 2017).

308.definition: Theoretical structures representing common types of arguments used in everyday discourse (Walton, Reed & Macagno 2008).

309.definition: A specific blind spot or systematic preference identified in large language models (Wang et al. 2023).

310.definition: A decoding strategy that improves chain-of-thought reasoning in language models by sampling multiple reasoning paths and selecting the most consistent answer (Wang et al. 2022).

311.definition: An advanced attention mechanism for language models designed to improve focus and reasoning, analogous to human deliberate thought (Weston & Sukhbaatar 2023).

312.definition: An approach to designing assessments specifically intended to inform and improve student performance rather than just audit it (Wiggins 1998).

313.definition: Systems composed of multiple interacting intelligent agents (Wooldridge 2009).

314.definition: A framework where multiple agents interact through debate, though it is subject to specific failure modes (Wynn, Satija & Hadfield 2025).

315.definition: A failure mode in AI agents where the effectiveness of instructions diminishes as the prompt becomes overloaded (Yeager.ai 2023).

316.definition: A phenomenon in AI agents where information from the context unintentionally interferes with the agent's specific task or instruction set (Yeager.ai 2023).

317.definition: A security vulnerability where malicious instructions are introduced into a large language model through retrieved or external data (Yi et al. 2025).

318.definition: An AI-driven architecture that utilizes directed acyclic graphs to structure reasoning processes (Zhang et al. 2024).

319.definition: A type of knowledge corruption attack targeting the Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) processes of Large Language Models (Zou et al. 2024).
